Definition: a primary preposition; to or into (indicating the point reached or entered), of place, time, or (figuratively) purpose (result, etc.); also in adverbial phrases:--(abundant-)ly, against, among, as, at, (back-)ward, before, by, concerning, + continual, + far more exceeding, for (intent, purpose), fore, + forth, in (among, at, unto, -so much that, -to), to the intent that, + of one mind, + never, of, (up-)on, + perish, + set at one again, (so) that, therefore(-unto), throughout, til, to (be, the end, -ward), (here-)until(-to), …ward, (where-)fore, with. Often used in composition with the same general import, but only with verbs (etc.) expressing motion (literally or figuratively).
BiblicalUsage: Into is the word of movement and destination, and the New Testament uses it for baptism, belief, and belonging. Jesus sends His disciples to baptise all nations into the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, John says those who receive Him become children of God, and Peter tells the crowd to be baptised for the remission of sins. Paul says we are baptised into Jesus Christ and into His death, so the little word carries us from outside to inside.
TheologicalSignificance: I believe faith moves a person into Christ, not just toward Him, because baptism and belief both speak of entering, not of standing at the door. My position is that being in Christ is the whole of salvation, and this small word says it.
